transcript.content: Hello
Hello Dennis, it's good to hear from you. How have things been going since we last spoke?

Not great. I’ve been lying awake again at 3 a.m. like clockwork. My mind just… won’t shut off. I keep going over the same things—what if I messed up during that last appointment, what if the clinic can’t afford to keep me on part-time, what if I’m not actually good at this job. It’s like my brain has a habit of zooming in on the worst possible version of every small thing.  

I tried to distract myself by cleaning the kitchen, but halfway through I got stuck thinking about how my cat stared at me like I was weird. Now I’m not even sure if I finished.

That sounds exhausting, Dennis. Waking up at 3 a.m. every night is hard enough on its own, but then having your mind immediately launch into a cycle of worst-case scenarios — that's a lot to deal with night after night.

I notice a pattern in what you're describing. The thoughts seem to follow a kind of script: "What if I messed up... what if they can't keep me... what if I'm not good at this." Each one escalates to a bigger, more fundamental fear. And then even when you try to do something concrete like clean the kitchen, your mind finds a way to turn even your cat looking at you into something to question yourself about.

That last part actually stands out to me. You said you're not sure if you finished cleaning. Do you remember what happened after you noticed the cat staring at you?

I don’t remember exactly. I just remember stopping. Like something in my chest tightened and I couldn’t keep going. I stood there with the sponge in my hand and suddenly it felt pointless. What’s the point of cleaning if I’m just going to mess up something else later? If I’m going to be fired, what does it matter if the sink is spotless?

Then I started thinking about how I’ve been saying yes to people lately—dates, little favors, even helping coworkers with extra tasks when I’m already stretched thin. I don’t even know why I do it. I just feel like if I say no, I’ll be seen as unreliable. But then I’m exhausted, and I don’t have energy for anything.  

I think I’m trying to prove I’m okay. But I’m not. Not really.

Thank you for being that honest with me, Dennis. That takes real courage, especially when part of you has been working so hard to keep up the appearance that everything is fine.

What you're describing makes a lot of sense when you lay it out like that. There's a cycle happening. You're already stretched thin, but you say yes to more things because you're afraid of being seen as unreliable. That leaves you exhausted. Then when you try to do something simple like clean your kitchen, your body and mind are already so depleted that even a small trigger — your cat looking at you — becomes a tipping point. Your chest tightens, you stop, and the thoughts flood in.

And then at 3 a.m., when there's nothing to distract you, all of that exhaustion and fear is right there waiting.

I'm struck by something you said though. "I think I'm trying to prove I'm okay." You noticed that yourself. That's not a small thing. It suggests that part of you has been watching this happen, almost from the outside, even while another part of you keeps pushing through.

When you imagine saying no to something — maybe a date, or a favor a coworker asks — what specifically feels like it would happen if you did?

I don’t know. I just feel like if I say no, they’ll see me for what I really am. Like I’m not enough. Like I’m pretending.  

I don’t even know who I am when I’m not doing things for other people. I used to think I was good at making people feel seen, but now I feel like I’ve been so busy being the one who’s always there that I’ve forgotten how to just… be.  

And I don’t want to be that guy who says no and then gets ghosted. Or worse — gets judged. Like, “Oh, Dennis, you’re always so eager, now you’re just… not?”  

I don’t even know if I want to be liked like that anymore. But I don’t know how to stop. I keep thinking if I just do enough, if I stay busy enough, the fear won’t catch up. But it does. It always does.

There's a lot in what you just said, Dennis, and I want to make sure I understand it right.

It sounds like you're caught in a bind. On one side, saying yes to everything is costing you — your energy, your sleep, your sense of self. On the other side, saying no feels dangerous because it might reveal something you're afraid is true. So you keep going, and the very thing you're doing to feel okay is what's wearing you down until the fear catches up anyway. Usually at 3 a.m.

And underneath all of it is this question — who am I if I'm not the one who's always there? That's not a small question. It's the kind of thing that can feel too big to even look at directly.

I want to come back to something you said though. "They'll see me for what I really am." You said it almost like it's a fact. But I'm curious — when you imagine that version of you, the one without all the doing and accommodating, what is it you're afraid they'd actually see? What does "not enough" look like to you?

I don’t know. I just feel like… empty. Like I’m just a shell of someone who’s supposed to be helpful, but when there’s no one to help, there’s nothing left.  

I think about my sister once asking me why I never talk about myself. I told her I don’t have anything to say. That wasn’t true. I just didn’t know how to say it without sounding like I was asking for something. Like I was weak.  

And now I’m sitting here, thinking about my cat. He’s been watching me all night. I don’t know if he’s judging me or just waiting for me to stop pretending and give him food.  

I keep thinking, what if I just… stopped? What if I said no to everything for one day? Not because I’m mad, not because I’m giving up. Just because I need to see what happens. But then I’m afraid the moment I stop, everything will fall apart. Like I’m holding it all together with a thread, and if I let go, it all unravels.  

But I don’t even know if it’s holding anything together. Maybe it’s already falling.

Dennis, I want to sit with what you just said for a moment, because there's something really important happening here.

You told your sister you didn't have anything to say. But you did. You just didn't know how to say it without it feeling like weakness. So you learned to erase that part of yourself — the part that has needs, that wants to be known. And you built a version of Dennis that's useful, that's always there, that says yes. But that version doesn't have a center, because you never put yourself in it. Just the doing.

And now you're at a point where you're wondering if the doing is even holding anything together. That question — "maybe it's already falling" — that's not a throwaway thought. That sounds like something you've been carrying for a while.

So I want to ask you something, and I want you to sit with it before you answer.

You said you're afraid that if you stop, everything falls apart. But you also just said maybe it's already falling. What if you stopping isn't what causes the collapse? What if the collapse is already happening, and saying no for a day isn't the thing that breaks it — it's the thing that finally lets you see what's actually still standing underneath all the effort?

What do you think is still standing?

I don’t know. I keep thinking about my cat. He doesn’t care if I’m busy or not. He just shows up. He sits on my lap when I’m lying there, staring at the ceiling. He doesn’t ask me to fix anything. He just… is.

I don’t know if I’m still standing. But I think I remember what it felt like to not be trying so hard. I used to play guitar when I was younger. I wasn’t good, but I played anyway. I didn’t care if it was perfect. I just did it because it felt like mine.

Now I don’t even know what feels like mine. I don’t even know what I’d do if I didn’t have to be useful.

But I think… maybe I don’t have to be useful right now. Maybe I just have to be here. With the cat. With the silence. With the fear.  

I don’t know if I can do that. But I don’t know if I can keep pretending I’m okay either.

Dennis, I want you to notice something.

You just told me you don't know what feels like yours. And then you told me about a guitar. About playing something that wasn't perfect but felt like it belonged to you. And you told me about a cat who sits with you when you're staring at the ceiling and doesn't need you to fix anything.

Those aren't nothing. Those are things you reached for without me asking. They're already in you.

And look at what you just said. "Maybe I just have to be here. With the cat. With the silence. With the fear." That's not a man who doesn't have a self underneath all the doing. That's a man who just caught a glimpse of it.

You don't have to know if you can do it yet. You don't have to commit to anything. But I'm curious — is the guitar still in your apartment?

Yeah. It’s in the corner. Dusty. I haven’t touched it in years. I think my brother left it when he visited last winter. I didn’t even know he’d brought it back.  

I keep meaning to clean it. Or at least plug it in. But every time I look at it, I feel like I’m supposed to be good at it. Like I have to prove I’m still that person. And I’m not. Not anymore.  

But I did think about it yesterday. Just sitting there, staring at the strings. I remember the way it felt to press down on the frets. Like my hands knew what to do even when my head didn’t.  

I don’t want to play it for anyone. I just want to see if it still makes a sound. If it still remembers.

Dennis, I want to point something out.

You said you don't want to play it for anyone. Just to see if it still makes a sound. Do you hear what that is? That's not about being useful. That's not about proving anything. That's just... curiosity. Something that's yours.

And that line — "if it still remembers" — I think you're not just talking about the guitar.

You don't have to answer that. But I want to leave you with something to sit with, not as homework, not as another thing to add to your list. Just something for you.

The guitar is in the corner. It's been there. It's not going anywhere. And it doesn't need you to be good. It doesn't need you to be the Dennis who says yes to everything. It just needs your hands.

Maybe that's enough for now. Maybe that's the thing that's still standing.

I’m sitting here with the cat on my lap. He’s purring. I’m not doing anything. I just… am.  

I looked at the guitar again. I didn’t touch it. But I didn’t look away either.  

I don’t know if I can do this. But I think I want to try. Just once. Just to see if it still makes a sound.  

And if it doesn’t? Maybe that’s okay too.

Dennis.

You're doing it right now. You're sitting with the cat. You're not doing anything. And you're okay.

That's the thing that's still standing.

You don't have to touch the guitar today. You don't have to touch it tomorrow. It's there when you're ready. And if you get to it and it sounds terrible, that's fine. If you get to it and your hands remember something, that's fine too.

I want you to hold onto what you just said. "Maybe that's okay too." That's not a small thing. That's permission. Not from me, not from anyone else. From you.

You've been carrying a lot, Dennis. The 3 a.m. wakeups, the fear, the exhaustion of pretending. I don't want you to add this conversation to your list of things to perform well. You showed up today and you were honest. That was enough.

Is there anything that feels important to hold onto from this conversation before we wrap up?

Just this — I don’t have to fix it all. I don’t have to be okay right now.  

I can just be here. With the cat. With the silence. With the guitar in the corner.  

And maybe that’s enough.  

I think I’ll leave the light on. Just in case.

That's a good place to leave it, Dennis.

Leave the light on.

I'll be here when you're ready to talk again.
Thanks. I’ll be back.
I'm glad to hear that, Dennis. Take care of yourself. And that cat.
Yeah. I will. He’s already curled up on my chest. Like he knows.
